content:
Hi all,
I've recently been working with to_additive-related features. It looks like the Lean engine does some guessing to determine the target name when the attribute doesn't specify one explicitly.
Because of that guessing, it seems fairly easy for an unexpected statement name on the usage side to end up changing the original to_additive target.

Here's a minimal compiling example:

import Mathlib

@[to_additive]
theorem foo_mul_comm {α : Type*} [CommMonoid α] (a b : α) : a * b = b * a :=
  mul_comm a b

-- `foo_add_comm` is generated automatically:
#check foo_add_comm

Because no explicit target name was given, Lean guesses foo_add_comm from foo_mul_comm. The concern is that this guessing can be sensitive to naming on the usage side, which may silently change which declaration the attribute targets.
A few questions:

  1. Is this guessing behavior documented anywhere in detail?
  2. Is there a recommended way to make target resolution more predictable (e.g., always passing an explicit name)?
  3. Would it be reasonable to treat this as a bug / feature request, or is it working as intended?

Thanks!

You could always specify a name if you don't like/trust the name guessing.
I'm not sure what the mwe is showing, this looks like standard to_additive usage.

I think the names are pretty predictable, but the exact details are in GuessName.lean, and you're probably looking for these dictionaries that map parts of names. You can edit these dictionaries (or use to_additive_name_hint foo bar) to affect the guessed names.

btw this is a Mathlib thing, not a Lean thing.

Your response raises a fundamental issue: if we cannot trust the Lean engine, we are expected to implement our own solutions. This implies that the Lean engine hasn't reached a sufficient level of trustworthiness, forcing developers to build workarounds. This brings me back to my original question: should this behavior be considered a bug that needs to be addressed in the future?
This topic was moved here from #lean4 > to_additive name guessing and downstream surprises by Kevin Buzzard.

I've moved this to mathlib4 because on the face of it, it seems to be an observation about to_additive. @Linfeng Song Lean is a programming language and it is possible to write Lean code which makes random declarations if you run it, like you are doing with @[to_additive]. I am not clear about whether you are objecting to "Lean is a programming language" (this is not a bug) or to "to_additive makes new declarations" (in which case the discussion belongs here).

@Linfeng Song Question 1 and 2 are already answered (both yes). To be clear, the answer to question 3 is “the mathlib maintainers think this behavior is fine and can be trusted, but you're free to disagree”.

Lean engine is not at trust level

to_additive is in mathlib, not Lean engine.
I'm not sure what you mean by "can be trusted". You can't prove untrue things by making weird to_additive declarations. The worst you can do is mislead.

It really depends on how we define 'weird' behavior. In the case of to_additive, the code may look correct on the surface, but its actual behavior can be flawed. For example, if two multiplicative keywords are defined within the same module, the environment will contain two corresponding additive statements, making it ambiguous which one should be chosen as the target. This ambiguity is precisely why this Lean feature is referred to as 'guesswork.' In more complex scenarios, where an environment opens multiple modules with conflicting additive definitions, determining the correct mapping becomes even more difficult.
The answer to question 3 is indeed: This is a feature and it is working as intended. You can hover over the to_additive attribute to see what new declaration it generated.

This feature only assists with development in VS Code and does not contribute to runtime stability, because the core Mathlib to_additive macro relies on the same kind of heuristic guesswork as an AI. This issue is distinct from runtime type matching; while type matching relies on object identifier alignment, to_additive operates via string pattern matching without any clearly defined logic or constraints

Here is an example demonstrating the confusing behavior of the to_additive name mapping. I copied an original Mathlib4 module and added a suffix to a structure name to test how the mapping behaves. While it only appended the suffix to the structure name itself, to_additive internally altered a field name within the structure, even though that field belongs to a different base structure. Specifically, to_additive generated ih.add_₂ on the last line. I expected it not to use the name add_₂ because no such modification was intended.

For now, my best guess at a response is “if you don't expect the field to be renamed to add_₂, maybe you should change your expectation”. Concrete suggestions to improve the LSP output may be more likely to be accepted.
